creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Signal Processing
FFT
Fourier Transform
Frequency Analysis
dublinCore.description: A sine-wave generator with its live FFT: a triggered 20 ms window of the waveform in the time domain on top and its magnitude spectrum from 0 to 2100 Hz below, with frequency and amplitude sliders, Start/Pause and Reset.
relation: Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis

learningObjectives: Explain that the FFT decomposes a time-domain waveform into the frequencies it contains
Predict that raising the frequency slider shortens the period in the time-domain plot and shifts the spectral peak to the right in the frequency-domain plot
Predict that increasing the amplitude slider raises both the waveform and the spectral peak in proportion while leaving the peak's frequency unchanged
Distinguish the time-domain display, which plots amplitude against time, from the frequency-domain display, which plots magnitude against frequency
Identify the frequency of a pure sine wave from the location of its single spectral peak and from the number of cycles in the 20 ms window

misconceptions.misconception: A higher frequency makes a taller spike
misconceptions.correction: Frequency moves the spike sideways; only the amplitude changes its height
misconceptions.evidence: At amplitude 0.5, moving the frequency from 220 Hz to 880 Hz moves the spike to the right while its height stays near 0.5

misconceptions.misconception: The time-domain wave and the frequency-domain spike should look alike
misconceptions.correction: The two plots show different information: how the signal changes over time versus which frequencies it contains
misconceptions.evidence: A smooth wave with 8.8 cycles in the window becomes one narrow spike at 440 Hz

misconceptions.misconception: The FFT creates the frequencies it displays
misconceptions.correction: The FFT only reveals frequencies that are already in the signal
misconceptions.evidence: Press Pause: the signal goes silent and the spike decays to nothing

accessibility.screenReaderScript: A sine-wave generator with its FFT. The top plot shows the waveform over a 20 millisecond window; the bottom plot shows its magnitude spectrum from 0 to 2100 Hz. Press Start, then move the Frequency and Amplitude sliders to see the spectral peak move and change height.

controls.label: Frequency
controls.description: Sets the frequency of the sine wave

controls.label: Amplitude
controls.description: Sets the peak amplitude of the sine wave (the speaker plays it at half this level)

controls.label: Start / Pause
controls.description: Starts audio on the first click, then toggles the tone and the live analysis on and off

controls.label: Reset
controls.description: Returns the sliders to 440 Hz and amplitude 0.5

visualElements.description: Time-domain plot (green): a 20 ms window of the waveform, triggered on a rising zero crossing, with amplitude gridlines at 0.5 and 1
Frequency-domain plot (purple): magnitude spectrum from 0 to 2100 Hz with a gold marker on the strongest bin
Status indicator (RUNNING / PAUSED), strongest-bin frequency and magnitude, sample rate and bin width

model.description: An oscillator produces x(t) = A sin(2 pi f t). The browser's analyser (via p5.sound) applies a Blackman window and a 16384-point FFT; the sketch plots the magnitude normalised so that an amplitude-1 sine centred on a bin reaches 1.
equations: x(t) = A sin(2 pi f t)
X[k] = (1/N) sum_{n=0}^{N-1} w[n] x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}
algorithms: Rising zero-crossing trigger for the time-domain display
limitations: The read-out reports the centre of the strongest bin, so it can differ from the slider frequency by up to half a bin (about 1.5 Hz at 48 kHz)
A tone between two bins reads up to about 12% low because of the Blackman window

instructionalStrategies: Worksheet table relating amplitude to wave height and spike height
Connecting musical pitch to spike position
extensions: Add a second oscillator and observe two spikes
Compare FFT sizes to see how bin width changes the peak width
